issues.description: Constructor signature for StockIngredient is inconsistent across artifacts: the problem statement UML and the solution expect a 3-parameter constructor StockIngredient(String, int, int), but the template repository provides only a 4-parameter constructor StockIngredient(String, int, int, boolean). This will prevent students from instantiating StockIngredient using the constructor described in the specification and used in the solution (e.g., new StockIngredient(name, price, quantity)) and will cause compile errors when they implement SealSaloon.acceptSupplyDelivery as instructed.
issues.suggestedFix: Add or overload a 3-argument constructor StockIngredient(String name, int price, int quantity) to the template StockIngredient class (or modify the template to match the constructor signature shown in the problem statement). The 3-arg constructor can delegate to the existing 4-arg constructor (e.g., passing a default boolean) or implement the same validation logic as in the solution. This will align the template with the specification and allow students to instantiate StockIngredient as described.

issues.description: The problem statement and solution expect a StockIngredient constructor with signature StockIngredient(String, int, int) but the template provides only a constructor with an extra boolean parameter (StockIngredient(String, int, int, boolean)). This mismatch creates a direct obstacle for students: the exercise text and UML show creating StockIngredient instances with three arguments (and Main in the template also uses a three-arg constructor in comments), while the template's available constructor requires four arguments. Students implementing SealSaloon.acceptSupplyDelivery or following the example in Main will be confused or face compilation errors because the intended three-argument constructor is missing.
issues.suggestedFix: Provide an overloaded three-argument constructor in the template matching the problem statement and solution: public StockIngredient(String name, int price, int quantity) { this(name, price, quantity, false); } or adjust the template constructor to accept (String, int, int) so students can instantiate StockIngredient(name, price, quantity) as described in the UML and examples.
